newsitem.title: USA: Antitrust not seen stopping US bank consolidation.
newsitem.headline: Antitrust not seen stopping US bank consolidation.

text.p: U.S. antitrust laws are unlikely to stand in the way of the continued consolidation of the banking industry, an economist for the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System said on Friday.

"While the demise of antitrust in banking is not imminent, continued application of the antitrust statutes should not become a barrier to a continuation of the ongoing consolidation movement in banking," senior Fed economist Dean Amel said at a conference here sponsored by the Chicago Federal Reserve Bank.
But the Fed and other bank regulators will still block anticompetitive mergers, Amel said. The ongoing merger wave "suggests an active business climate in this area in the short run."
"While some major horizontal bank mergers will be blocked for antitrust reasons, that will not stop the continued decline in the number of banks in this country," Amel said.

Some computer simulations suggest that the 7,300 banks in the United States could drop to six without ever violating the Fed's bank merger guidelines, he added. One of the simulation ended with the same handful of banks in each of 2,000 markets.
Technological changes may eventually cause the Fed to reassess the antitrust criteria it uses to assess bank mergers, Amel said.

Currently, the Fed only includes banks when reviewing the amount of competition in a market following a merger. But with more non-banks offering financial services, and technology erasing geographic barriers, the so-called clustering policy could be changed in the future, Amel said.

"If future surveys of households and small businesses show a substantial weakening of the clustering of bank services, then the Board might abandon the cluster and analyze the effect of competition on each of multiple bank products," Amel said.

Including non-banks in the antitrust assessment might make the process less predictable, however, Amel said. "It might be difficult for bankers to predict the stance of the antitrust enforcement agencies in individual bank product markets," Amel said.
